01 · HANDIC.APPUX/UI · Accessibility · Mobile App

Booking an event shouldn’t mean searching for accessibility information.

Handic.app explores a more accessible event-booking experience, helping wheelchair users find relevant accessibility information throughout the event discovery and booking journey.

Role
UX/UI Designer
Project
University project
Focus
Accessibility · Event booking
Output
Mobile app · Landing page

The problem

Finding the ticket was easy.
Finding the accessibility information wasn’t.

For wheelchair users, planning an event can involve more than choosing a date and buying a ticket. Essential information such as wheelchair access, accessible seating, parking and venue facilities may require additional searching before someone can confidently plan their visit.

Accessibility information should be part of the event experience — not something users have to search for separately.

Designing with a real need in mind.

The project focused on understanding the needs of wheelchair users attending live events, including the information they may need before deciding whether an event and venue are suitable for them.

Shaping the experience.

Before developing the final visual interface, I explored how event discovery and information could be structured in a clear and accessible way.

The core idea

Accessibility information, where it matters.

One of the central ideas behind Handic.app was to make important venue accessibility information easier to find as part of the event experience itself.

Wheelchair seating, nearby restrooms and ramps, elevator access and companion seating — together within the event details.

From discovery to booking.

The final interface brings event discovery, event information, accessibility details and seat selection into one consistent visual experience.

Beyond the app.

The Handic.app visual identity was also extended into a supporting landing page, carrying the same bold, concert-inspired language into the web experience.

Reflection

What I took from it.

This project made me think more carefully about where accessibility information appears in a user journey — not simply whether it exists. It encouraged me to treat accessibility as part of the core experience from the beginning, rather than something added around it later.
